passage: Vaibhav had wanted a motorbike since he started driving the tractor on his uncle's farm outside Satara. The dealer in town smiled and said, "Zero down payment, small EMI, sign here." Jyoti, his cousin who kept accounts for the dairy co-op, asked to see the paper first. She sat on the dealer's bench with a pencil and added up the monthly payments for three years. The total was much more than the bike's price. "The EMI is small because it runs long," she said. "And if you miss one, there's a late charge on top." Vaibhav stared at the figure. He had planned only for the monthly amount. He didn't sign that day. He went home to count what he could put down first.

qa.q: Who added up the monthly payments?
qa.a: Jyoti, his cousin who keeps accounts for the dairy co-op, added them up.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav realise when he saw Jyoti's total?
qa.a: He realised he had only thought about the monthly amount and had not understood how much more the loan would cost overall.

qa.q: What went well in how Vaibhav handled the offer?
qa.a: He let someone check the paper and did not sign on the spot, giving himself time to think about saving first.

qa.q: How might the dealer see Vaibhav walking away?
qa.a: The dealer may see a lost sale, since the easy offer depended on buyers looking only at the small monthly payment.

grounding: Shows a young man learning that a small EMI over a long period adds up to much more than the price.

passage: Dalia got her first credit card in her second year at university in Valencia. The statement came with a line in bold: minimum payment due. It was tiny, so she paid it and felt responsible. Three months later her balance had barely moved. She showed Xin, her flatmate, who studied economics. Xin pointed at a smaller line she'd skipped: the interest charged. "You're paying mostly interest," Xin said. "The rest keeps growing on itself." Dalia felt a hot rush of embarrassment. She cut the card up that night, which Xin said was one way, and taped the statement to her wardrobe door. She decided to ask the student money advice office what her options were.

qa.q: What was printed in bold on Dalia's statement?
qa.a: The minimum payment due was printed in bold.

qa.q: How did Dalia feel when Xin explained the interest, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, described as a hot rush, because she had believed paying the minimum was responsible.

qa.q: What sensible next step did Dalia take?
qa.a: She planned to ask the student money advice office about her options instead of guessing alone.

qa.q: What would change if Dalia had read the interest line from the start?
qa.a: She would have seen early that the minimum barely touched her balance and could have changed course sooner.

grounding: Shows a student discovering how credit card interest compounds when only the minimum is paid.

passage: In the hostel common room, Eshaan kept refreshing his phone. Jomon, a senior who helped run the hostel's money-awareness evenings, noticed his leg bouncing. "Everything okay?" Eshaan showed him a message from an instant loan app: pay today or they would contact his contacts. He had borrowed a little for fees, then more to repay the first loan. "It kept growing," he said quietly. Jomon didn't lecture. He said threats like that were a known pattern and that Eshaan should not borrow again to cover it. He walked him to the warden's office and helped him find the college's student support cell. Eshaan's shoulders dropped a little as he wrote down the timing. "I thought I was the only one," he said.

qa.q: Why had Eshaan first borrowed money from the app?
qa.a: He borrowed a little to pay fees.

qa.q: What does Eshaan's bouncing leg and quiet voice suggest?
qa.a: They suggest he was anxious and ashamed about the debt and the threatening messages.

qa.q: How did Jomon support Eshaan well?
qa.a: He stayed calm, did not lecture, and took him to the warden and the student support cell so trusted people could help.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's family see the situation if he had kept hiding it?
qa.a: They might only learn about it through the lender's threats, which would likely feel far more frightening than hearing it from him first. 🫂

grounding: Shows a student caught in a growing debt cycle from borrowing to repay loans, and being guided to trusted help.

passage:
Hey Eshaan,
You said you're getting your first credit card next month, so let me tell you what happened to me. Last year I bought a phone on my card and paid only the 'minimum due' each month because it seemed small. I thought I was fine. Then I actually read the statement. Interest was being charged on the whole unpaid balance, and the next month on that interest too. After eight months I owed more than the phone had cost, even though I had paid every single month. I felt stupid and scared. I told Appa, which was awful, and we sat with the statement to understand it and make a plan to clear it. So read the statement, understand how the interest works before you swipe, and if something doesn't add up, ask someone you trust or the bank. Don't be me.
Chinmay

qa.q: What did Chinmay buy on the card?
qa.a: A phone.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel when Chinmay finally read the statement?
qa.a: Stupid and scared, because Chinmay owed more than the phone cost despite paying every month.

qa.q: What does Chinmay want Eshaan to do before using a credit card?
qa.a: Read the statement, understand how interest builds on an unpaid balance, and ask a trusted person or the bank if something does not add up.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt when Chinmay told him?
qa.a: Probably worried and maybe disappointed, but willing to sit with Chinmay and make a plan, which shows care.

grounding: An email shows a young adult explaining from experience how card interest compounds when only the minimum is paid.

passage: Sachin, you asked why I freaked out when you mentioned that instant loan app. Okay, story time. In second year I needed money for a laptop repair before exams. An app offered 'instant approval, no paperwork'. I tapped yes in five minutes. What I didn't read: a big processing fee cut from the amount, and a charge for every day I was late. I missed one due date by a week, and suddenly the total was almost double. Then they started calling my contacts. That was the worst part, my aunt getting a call saying 'Kashish has unpaid dues'. I was shaking. My mother helped me pay it off, and a lawyer friend of hers helped us report the harassment. Now I read every loan term twice: interest, fees, late charges. If it's instant and easy, I get suspicious.

qa.q: What did Kashish need the money for?
qa.a: A laptop repair before exams.

qa.q: What was the worst part for Kashish, and how did it feel?
qa.a: The app calling Kashish's contacts, including the aunt; Kashish was left shaking and ashamed.

qa.q: What does Kashish do now when a loan offer appears?
qa.a: Kashish reads every term twice, especially interest, fees and late charges, and treats 'instant and easy' as a warning sign.

qa.q: How might Kashish's aunt have felt getting that call?
qa.a: Surprised and worried, and perhaps embarrassed on Kashish's behalf.

grounding: A young adult tells a friend how a quick loan with hidden fees became a debt trap and how they got out with help.

passage: I'm Lalremsiami, and I shared a flat with Usha in Guwahati the year she got her first credit card. I can only tell you what I saw. For the first months she used it for everything: phone, clothes, dinners with the office crowd. When the bill came she paid the "minimum due" and looked pleased, as if the problem was solved. In March I saw her at the table with the statement and a calculator, very quiet. The total had barely gone down; the interest line was bigger than the amount she had paid off. She said, half to herself, "I've been paying them to borrow." That week she stopped using the card and put it in a drawer. Then she booked a session with the bank's customer adviser and asked her cousin, a chartered accountant, to go through it with her. She stopped joining the Friday dinners for a while.

qa.q: What did Usha pay when the bill came in the first months?
qa.a: The minimum due.

qa.q: What might Usha have been feeling at the table with the calculator?
qa.a: Usha was probably shocked and worried to see the interest outgrowing her payments, and perhaps embarrassed.

qa.q: Which of Usha's steps pointed her towards reliable help?
qa.a: Booking a session with the bank's adviser and asking her cousin, a chartered accountant, to go through the statement with her.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami see Usha's change from the outside?
qa.a: Lalremsiami notices the quietness and the missed Friday dinners, and seems concerned but respectful of how seriously Usha took it.

grounding: A flatmate observes a young woman discover how interest compounds when only the minimum credit card payment is made.

passage:
September. Simran bought a new phone on a "no-cost EMI" over twelve months. It felt free. In October she added headphones on another plan from the same shop. Her friend Farida raised an eyebrow. "Did you read the processing fee?" Simran hadn't.
December. Her stipend came late, and she missed one EMI by four days. The late fee and the extra interest on the missed amount made her stomach turn. Farida, who studies commerce, sat with her on the hostel bed and helped her read the loan agreement line by line: processing fee, penalty rate, what a missed payment does to a credit record.
February. Simran called the lender and moved the EMI date to the day after her stipend arrives. She also told her mother what had happened, which was harder than any call. She still has the phone. She hasn't taken another EMI since.

qa.q: How many days late was Simran's missed EMI?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when she saw the late fee and extra interest?
qa.a: Simran felt a sick, anxious drop in her stomach, realising the 'free' EMI had real costs.

qa.q: What helped Simran understand the loan, and who else could she turn to?
qa.a: Reading the agreement line by line with Farida showed the fees and penalties; before any future credit she could also check with a qualified adviser or her mother.

qa.q: How might Simran's mother feel hearing about it?
qa.a: Her mother might feel worried at first, but also glad Simran told her honestly and is dealing with it.

grounding: Over months, a student learns how EMIs, fees and missed payments work after a 'no-cost' purchase goes wrong.

passage: Parul, you asked why your Alka Bua gets so angry about those instant-loan apps. It's because of your Mohit Chacha, when he was twenty-one. He borrowed five thousand from one app for a college trip. The interest, he found later, was many times what a bank charges, and fees were cut before the money even arrived. When he couldn't repay in a week, he borrowed from a second app to pay the first. Then a third. Within two months he owed several times what he had borrowed, and they started calling his contacts, me included. That's how I found out. I still see his face in our kitchen, grey with shame. The turning point wasn't money. It was him finally showing us every message. That same evening we went together to the police cyber cell, and then to a lawyer friend. It took a year to settle. So, Parul, when anything online says "instant", come and talk to me first.

qa.q: How much did Mohit borrow from the first app?
qa.a: Five thousand.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling in the kitchen?
qa.a: Mohit felt deeply ashamed, his face grey, after the debt spiralled and his contacts were called.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Mohit's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Mohit showing the family every message, because it ended the secrecy and led them to the cyber cell and a lawyer that same evening.

qa.q: How did Alka experience getting a call about her brother's debt?
qa.a: Alka was probably shocked and frightened, and later angry at the apps, which is why she still reacts so strongly.

grounding: An aunt tells how her brother at twenty-one fell into a debt trap of instant-loan apps and got out with family and professional help.

passage:
It was the last day to pay his college fees, and Anand was short by Rs 15,000. An ad popped up: "Instant loan in 5 minutes! No documents!"
He downloaded the app. It asked for access to his contacts and photos. The interest rate was in tiny print. It worked out to a huge amount per year, with extra charges for any delay.
His sister Sudha called. He told her.
"Stop. Don't take it," she said. "Those apps harass people's contacts when they can't pay."
"But the fees—"
"Let's call the college accounts office first. And talk to Papa's bank about a proper education loan."
The accounts office gave him a week's extension. Anand deleted the app.

qa.q: How much was Anand short for his fees?
What was Anand feeling when he downloaded the app?
qa.a: Anand felt desperate and pressured by the fee deadline.

qa.q: What choices did Sudha point Anand toward instead of the loan app?
qa.a: Asking the college for an extension and talking to a bank about a proper education loan.

qa.q: How does Sudha see instant loan apps?
qa.a: Sudha sees them as risky traps that can harass contacts when people can't pay.

grounding: Under deadline pressure a young man avoids a predatory loan app with his sister's help.

passage:
In her first job in Mumbai, Sarita got a credit card. She used it for clothes, dinners and a new phone. Each month she paid only the "minimum due". It seemed manageable.
Six months later, her colleague Alka saw her statement on the desk. "Sarita, the total is bigger than when you started."
"But I've been paying every month!"
"Only the minimum. The rest keeps collecting interest. That's how it grows."
Sarita felt sick. She hadn't understood.
Alka suggested she stop using the card and talk to the bank or a qualified financial counsellor about a plan to clear it.
That weekend, Sarita cut the card in half and booked an appointment.

qa.q: What amount did Sarita pay each month?
qa.a: Only the "minimum due".

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when she learnt about the interest?
qa.a: Sarita felt sick and shocked at how the debt had grown.

qa.q: What steps did Sarita take after understanding the problem?
qa.a: She stopped using the card and booked an appointment with the bank or a qualified counsellor.

qa.q: How does Alka see paying only the minimum?
qa.a: Alka sees it as a trap that lets interest keep growing.

grounding: A young woman learns how minimum credit card payments let debt compound.

passage:
"Kunal, you're buying the new phone on EMI? Your old one works fine."
"It's only Rs 3,000 a month, Gautam. Easy."
"For how long?"
"Eighteen months."
"And the total price?"
Kunal checked. "…Higher than the phone's price."
"That's interest and fees. Plus you already have your bike EMI."
Kunal sat back. "So two EMIs every month."
"And if your job changes?"
"Okay, that's scary."
"I'm not saying never. Just read the total, not just the monthly. And maybe ask your bank what it costs in total."
Kunal closed the app. "I'll keep the old phone for now."

qa.q: For how many months was the EMI?
qa.a: Eighteen months.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling on saying "that's scary"?
qa.a: Kunal felt worried and uneasy, seeing the risk of two EMIs.

qa.q: What did Gautam suggest Kunal look at?
qa.a: The total cost, not just the monthly payment, and asking the bank about it.

qa.q: How does Gautam see small EMIs?
qa.a: Gautam sees them as adding up to more than they seem and becoming risky if income changes.

grounding: Two young adults discuss how EMIs and interest add up.

passage:
At nineteen I got my first credit card, and I felt very grown-up. I bought a phone, some clothes, a trip with friends. Every month I paid the "minimum due", because the app made that button biggest.
After a year my sister Bhavna, who's an accountant, saw my statement on the table. She went quiet. "Uday, do you know how much interest you've paid?"
I didn't. She showed me: interest charged on interest, every month. The balance had barely moved, even though I'd paid something every time.
I felt stupid and scared. Bhavna didn't lecture. She sat with Papa and me that weekend, and we went to the bank together to understand the options. I cut up the card.
It took me a year and a half to clear. Now I read the full statement, every line.

qa.q: Which button did the app make biggest?
qa.a: The "minimum due" button.

qa.q: How did Uday feel when Bhavna showed the statement?
qa.a: Uday felt stupid and scared, realising how the debt had grown.

qa.q: What was sensible about how Bhavna handled it?
qa.a: She explained how the interest built up without lecturing and involved Papa and the bank so Uday could understand the options properly.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt going to the bank with Uday?
qa.a: Papa may have been worried but glad Uday asked for help instead of hiding the debt.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning how credit card interest compounds when paying only the minimum, and getting family and bank help.

passage:
Mentor's note. Binita, college finance-literacy cell.
Gautam came to our drop-in session shaking. Three months ago he took a quick loan from an app to pay for a laptop. The app showed a small weekly payment. It didn't show clearly how much he'd pay in total, or the late fees.
He'd missed two payments during exams. Now the total was much bigger than the laptop. The app had started messaging his contacts.
I told him that he hadn't been stupid, that these apps are designed to look easy. We read the loan terms together and worked out the true cost. I explained how a bank's loan or EMI scheme usually shows the full cost upfront, and that he should compare before agreeing to any loan.
He called his parents from my office. His father is coming tomorrow; I've connected them with our college's bank branch manager and the cyber cell for the harassing messages.

qa.q: Why did Gautam take the loan?
qa.a: To pay for a laptop.

qa.q: How was Gautam feeling when he came to the session?
qa.a: Gautam was frightened and ashamed, shaking because the debt had grown and the app was messaging his contacts.

qa.q: What steps did Binita take that were the right kind of help?
qa.a: Binita reduced his shame, read the terms with him, and connected him with his parents, a bank manager and the cyber cell, rather than giving personal money rules.

qa.q: How might Gautam's parents have felt getting his call?
qa.a: His parents were probably worried and upset, but relieved he told them before it got worse.

grounding: Illustrates a mentor helping a young adult understand how a loan app's fees and interest compounded, and connecting him with the right adults.

passage:
Thursday
Anjali writing. Almost bought the new phone today with "buy now, pay later". The screen said: "Just ₹2,000 a month!" Twelve months. I had my finger on the button.
Aparna Didi was sitting next to me. She said, "Multiply."
Twelve times two thousand is twenty-four thousand. The phone's price was twenty thousand. Plus a processing fee in tiny letters. And if I miss a month, a late charge.
"Where's the extra four thousand going?" she asked. Good question.
I felt a bit silly, and also a bit tricked. The whole screen was designed so I'd only see "₹2,000".
I didn't buy it. I'm going to ask Papa tomorrow what he thinks, and maybe the man at the bank. My old phone still works. It's just ugly.

qa.q: What did the screen say the monthly payment was?
qa.a: "Just ₹2,000 a month!" for twelve months.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel after multiplying the payments?
qa.a: Anjali felt silly and a bit tricked by how the screen hid the total.

qa.q: What was wise about Anjali's next steps?
qa.a: Anjali didn't buy on impulse and plans to ask Papa and someone at the bank before deciding.

qa.q: How might Aparna Didi feel about saying just one word, "Multiply"?
qa.a: Aparna Didi probably felt pleased that a simple nudge let Anjali work out the true cost herself.

grounding: Shows a young adult understanding the real cost of instalment payments and pausing to seek advice.
